clue.text: Surly person in college upset lawyers

indicators.note: something upset is turned over, so in a down entry the word is read bottom to top

blocks.note: C is a standard abbreviation for college
the Bar is the legal profession of barristers collectively

explanation.surface: A grumpy student, perhaps at a university college, has fallen out with the lawyers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in college' is just the scene-setting; the college supplies only its initial letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A crab is an informal word for a crabby, ill-tempered person, much as crabbed or crabby describes a sour temperament.

clue.text: Still reduced quantity of light around yard on a regular basis

definitions.note: the answer is usually an adjective; here it stands adverbially, as in 'everyday wear'

indicators.note: reduced means cut down, so the preceding word loses its final letter
around says one piece is wrapped about the other, surrounding it on both sides

blocks.note: still in the sense 'even' or 'yet', as in 'still more'
a ray is a narrow beam, a small amount of light
YD is the standard abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: A dull complaint about a reduced allowance of daylight in the yard, it seems, day after day.
explanation.walkthrough: EVEN loses its last letter to give EVE, and the yard abbreviation sits inside the beam of light.
explanation.definitionFit: Everyday describes what happens routinely or daily, which is what occurring on a regular basis means.

clue.text: Popular cycle runs involving fellows and stormy weather?

definitions.note: the question mark flags a definition by example: the answer is the quality of harsh weather

indicators.note: runs suggests letters running about loose, so the word before them is rearranged
involving means enclosing or wrapping in, so one group of letters goes inside the other

blocks.note: in means fashionable or popular
taken as written, the letters to be rearranged
fellows are men

explanation.surface: A popular bike ride takes in some chaps and a spot of rough weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' looks like part of the cycling scene, but it signals the rearrangement, which opens the word up so the fellows can sit in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Inclemency is harshness or severity, used above all of weather, so stormy conditions are an instance of it.

clue.text: Profit from performance delivered by soldiers

blocks.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
a turn is a performer's act or short performance

explanation.surface: A financial gain made from a show put on by the troops.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Engineers come first because the performance is 'delivered by' them, following on behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A return is the yield or gain on an investment, a synonym for profit.

clue.text: Program to take pain from running initially? I'll have anything for a quiet life

definitions.text: I'll have anything for a quiet life
definitions.note: a phrase in the person's own voice describing the answer, a noun

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word just before it

blocks.note: an app is a computer program
to ease is to relieve pain
the first letter of running

explanation.surface: Someone asks for software that will relieve the aches of jogging, then admits they just want peace.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a quotation: the voice of someone who gives in to keep the peace.
explanation.definitionFit: An appeaser makes concessions to avoid conflict, the attitude of someone who will concede anything for tranquillity.

clue.text: Great time, not at the start, the end

indicators.note: not at the start tells the solver to drop the opening letter of the phrase before it

blocks.note: a blast is informal for a really good time

explanation.surface: Someone sums up a great time that went downhill after the opening, right to the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great time' is a phrase, not two words: having a blast means having fun.
explanation.definitionFit: The last is the final part or conclusion, so it serves as a noun for the end.

clue.text: Lethargy defeats rising, requiring injection of pressure

indicators.note: rising in a down entry means the word is read upwards, from bottom to top
an injection goes inside, so the following letter is put into the word

blocks.note: routs are crushing defeats; as a verb, defeats
P is the scientific symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: A sluggish team keeps losing and needs a jab of pressure to wake up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' looks like recovery but is the turnaround signal for a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupor is a dazed, sluggish state, close in meaning to lethargy or torpor.

clue.text: Someone transcribing Asian menus in translation

indicators.note: translation turns words into something new, so the letters are rendered in a fresh order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A copyist working on menus from an Asian restaurant as they are translated.
explanation.definitionFit: An amanuensis is a literary assistant who writes from dictation or copies manuscripts, a scribe.

clue.text: Always taken aback about English reprisal

indicators.note: taken aback, read literally, means turned back, so the word runs right to left
about means surrounding, so the reversed word goes around the next piece

blocks.note: ever means always, as in 'ever hopeful'
ENG is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone forever shocked by an English act of retaliation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken aback' looks like surprise, but it turns EVER into REVE, which then wraps around the English abbreviation after its V.
explanation.definitionFit: Revenge is retaliation for a wrong, and a reprisal is exactly such an act of retaliation.

clue.text: Some expat bringing in hard worker? That's not for real

indicators.note: bringing in means taking inside, so the other pieces go into this one

blocks.note: a Pom is Australian slang for an English person, one kind of expat
H for hard, as on pencils
the worker ant is the crossword's stock worker

explanation.surface: A British emigrant employing a diligent labourer, who may turn out not to exist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some expat' is not a hidden word: it means one sort of expat, the Pom, Australian slang for a Briton.
explanation.definitionFit: Phantom as an adjective means illusory or imaginary, so it describes something that is not real.

clue.text: Rocky boulder is revealing avian pest

indicators.note: rocky means unsteady or shaky, so the letters that follow are shaken into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Turning over a rock reveals a creepy-crawly that troubles birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky boulder' reads as a natural pair, but 'Rocky' is the instruction for the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird louse is a small wingless parasite living in the plumage of birds, so it is a parasite of birds.

clue.text: Easy shot on the green - cheers near where the ball landed?

blocks.note: ta is British informal thanks, like cheers
the pin is the flagstick in the hole, which a good approach shot lands close to

explanation.surface: A golfer thanks the gods after an approach that stops by the flag, leaving a simple putt.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf the pin is the flagstick marking the hole; a ball landing next to it leaves a putt that only needs tapping.
explanation.definitionFit: A tap-in is a very short putt that the golfer can simply tap into the hole, an easy stroke.

clue.text: Architectural features Prince amends, incorporating pillars

indicators.note: incorporating means taking into its body, so one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for prince
edits means corrects or amends
carved male figures, telamons or atlantes, serve as pillars in classical buildings

explanation.surface: A royal tinkers with the design of a building's columns and ornaments.
explanation.walkthrough: Classical buildings sometimes use statues of men (atlantes) as columns, which is how pillars can be men.
explanation.definitionFit: Pediments are the triangular gables above classical porticoes and windows, decorative elements of building design.

clue.text: Medical expert, old man concealing damage, is appearing in court

indicators.note: concealing means hiding inside, so the next word goes within the one before
appearing in places one short word inside the abbreviation that follows

blocks.note: pa is a familiar word for father, one's old man
harm means damage
CT is the abbreviation for court
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly man in the dock hides the injury he caused, though he is a medical professional.
explanation.walkthrough: Two insertions: the damage goes inside the father, and the little word sits inside the court abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A pharmacist is trained in preparing and dispensing medicines, a professional with expertise in drugs.

clue.text: Strength in support of church

blocks.note: for means in support of, as in 'for or against'
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone shows great strength in backing their church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' joins the definition to the wordplay; the piece for backing is the short word that means in favour.
explanation.definitionFit: Force is power or strength, as in physical force.

clue.text: Heraldic symbol flourished over Europe, mostly tasteful

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the next word drops its final letter

blocks.note: fl., floruit, marks when someone flourished
EUR is an abbreviation for Europe
delish is a slang word for delicious, full of taste

explanation.surface: A heraldic emblem spread across Europe, a sign of refined taste.
explanation.walkthrough: fl. (floruit) is the scholarly abbreviation for 'flourished' beside a date. 'Tasteful' here means tasty, not refined.
explanation.definitionFit: The fleur-de-lis is the stylised lily used as a charge in heraldry, notably on the French royal arms.

clue.text: Are you up for some sport in afternoon? Yes, excited, name to be included

definitions.text: Are you up for some sport

indicators.note: excited means stirred up, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: letters to be rearranged
more letters for the rearrangement
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: An invitation to an afternoon game, answered with an eager yes.
explanation.walkthrough: The name's abbreviation is included among the letters before they are rearranged. The answer is the stock catchphrase of genteel country-house comedies.
explanation.definitionFit: The catchphrase is a cheery invitation to a game on the court, so it asks whether someone fancies playing.

clue.text: Alcoholic drink not entirely bad, but not to be taken that seriously

definitions.text: not to be taken that seriously

indicators.note: not entirely means falling short of the whole, so the last letter is removed

blocks.note: a flip is a drink of beaten egg with spirits or beer
pants is British slang for rubbish or bad

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs off a drink as not wholly bad, nothing to take too seriously.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'pants' means poor or rubbish ('that film was pants').
explanation.definitionFit: Flippant describes a light, unserious attitude, inappropriately casual about matters that deserve respect.

clue.text: Hooligan's about taken in, given order

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first piece goes around the second

blocks.note: a ned is Scottish slang for a young hooligan; the 's is 'has'
food taken in has been eaten

explanation.surface: A yob has been caught and is given his orders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooligan's about' reads as 'the hooligan is around'; a ned is a Scottish lout.
explanation.definitionFit: To neaten is to tidy up, so something neatened has been given order.

clue.text: Fictional doctor often considered real?

blocks.note: first meaning: Dr Leonard 'Bones' of Star Trek
second meaning: the genuine article, from the phrase 'the real ...'

explanation.surface: A television doctor so convincing that viewers think he is a real one.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half points to the idiom 'the real McCoy', meaning the genuine thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr McCoy is the ship's surgeon in Star Trek, and the idiom 'the real McCoy' pairs the name with 'real'.

clue.text: Civil Service accepting single copies?

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the abbreviation holds the next word inside

blocks.note: CS is the abbreviation for Civil Service
lone means single, solitary

explanation.surface: Government departments take on single copies of documents.
explanation.definitionFit: Clones are genetically identical replicas, hence exact copies of something.

clue.text: The best in American murders? Chilling things for consumption

indicators.note: in places the first piece inside the word that follows

blocks.note: ice is US slang for kill
the cream is the best part, as in 'cream of the crop'

explanation.surface: A grim question about whether the finest Americans are murderers, followed by a shiver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chilling' suggests horror but is literal: these are cold treats.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice creams are frozen desserts, so they are chilled things to eat.

clue.text: Politician in European country, powerful country?

indicators.note: in places the first piece inside the word for the country that follows

blocks.note: MP, Member of Parliament
Eire is the Irish name for Ireland

explanation.surface: A politician in an EU state asks whether it is a great power.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that an empire is a group of states under one power rather than strictly one country.
explanation.definitionFit: An empire is a large realm ruled by one sovereign power, a mighty state.

clue.text: Unwilling to follow Conservative ministers?

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
loth (or loath) means unwilling

explanation.surface: A question of whether government ministers are reluctant to back a Tory leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to follow' tells you the reluctant word comes after the party's letter. 'Ministers' are clergy, not cabinet members: the cloth is the clergy collectively.
explanation.definitionFit: The cloth is an idiom for the clergy as a body, as in 'a man of the cloth'.

clue.text: Hard work and energy will yield expectation

blocks.note: H for hard
an op is an opus, a work
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Effort and vigour will bring their own reward, the motto goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Hope is a feeling of expectation and desire that something will happen.

clue.text: Controlling influence elevated bad temper in unelected politician

indicators.note: in places the first pieces inside the word for the politician that follows

blocks.note: up means raised or elevated
a pet is a fit of sulking or bad temper
a peer sits in the House of Lords without being elected

explanation.surface: A raised temper in a member of the House of Lords exerts power behind the scenes.
explanation.walkthrough: A peer sits in the House of Lords, the UK's unelected upper chamber.
explanation.definitionFit: A puppeteer works the strings, so figuratively one who secretly controls others is a manipulating influence.

clue.text: Angry response within chamber is expected

indicators.note: within says the letters sit inside the next words, spanning them

blocks.note: the end of chamber, all of is, and the first letter of expected

explanation.surface: An angry reaction in parliament's chamber is to be expected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expected' supplies a letter and also links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To get a rise out of someone is to provoke an angry reaction from them.

clue.text: Stay abed? Wrong to cover skin over

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the word for skin is read backwards
to cover means to go over and around, so the wrong goes around the other piece

blocks.note: a sin is a wrong
peel is the skin of fruit

explanation.surface: Is it wrong to lie in bed and pull the covers over your skin?
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed skin goes between the S and the IN of the wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: To sleep in is to stay in bed later than usual, the idiom for staying abed.

clue.text: Cavalrymen capturing Australian attackers

indicators.note: capturing means seizing and holding, so the horsemen enclose the next letter

blocks.note: cavalrymen are horse riders
A is an abbreviation for Australian

explanation.surface: Mounted soldiers take an Australian prisoner during an assault.
explanation.definitionFit: Raiders are those who make sudden attacks on a place or enemy.
